# THEORYs with `tags` `learning-and-conditioning`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Learning and conditioning** — how organisms learn from contingencies and consequences — Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning, reinforcement and reward learning in brains, habit and goal-directed control, behaviour analysis and relational responding. Not machine learning, which is learning-theory or the anthology (ADR-025).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | Self as context is a learned deictic perspective | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) v2 | Expected engagement rewards lower later interest | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). By their study-by-study account, Cameron and Pierce's rival analysis found the same for this contingency (performance-independent rewards, −0.29), while disputing nearly everything else. Their 2001 reply (LIT-562), read here, re-codes 145 studies and finds it again: rewards offered for doing an interesting task lowered free choice, −0.35 across 57 studies. Active: both sides of the dispute find this effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-049.md) v2 | Control lowers motivation; competence info raises | Cognitive evaluation theory, as tested by Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)) and summarized by Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)): rewards, feedback, deadlines and choice affect intrinsic motivation through their "functional significance". Controlling events shift the perceived locus of causality outward and undermine it; informational ones affirm competence and enhance it, but only with a sense of autonomy. The meta-analytic pattern fits, and controlling versus informational positive feedback differ by d = −0.78 in four studies. Mediation by felt control is untested for rewards. Its rival, Cameron, Banko and Pierce's account (LIT-562), finds rewards tied to a score or to beating others do not undermine. Neither side has tested mediation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-050.md) | Psychological inflexibility is transdiagnostic | Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) model psychopathology as inflexibility: cognitive fusion supports experiential avoidance, which narrows behaviour. Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) give the mechanism: once a word stands in derived relation to an event it can carry that event's aversive functions, so private events become worth avoiding. Kashdan and Rottenberg ([LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md)) find inflexibility across depression and anxiety in cognitive, behavioural and physiological systems, and say its causal role is unknown. The evidence is correlational, small, mostly self-report and mostly from the model's authors, and the meta-analysis that would test it ([LIT-543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-543.md)) is unread, so Proposed. It is compatible with the loop account of disorder, not a rival to it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-062](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-062.md) v2 | Reliability, not a supervisor, arbitrates control | Daw, Niv & Dayan ([LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md)) cast habitual and goal-directed instrumental control as model-free caching and model-based search, and let behaviour follow whichever estimate is less uncertain; simulations reproduce the effects of over-training, task complexity and reward proximity on devaluation. Dayan & Berridge ([LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md)) show from instant revaluation of a salt cue that Pavlovian prediction also has a model-based form, and suggest the same reliability arbitration there. Both controllers pursue the same ends; neither is the irrational one. The instrumental half is qualitative simulation; the Pavlovian half of the arbitration is a suggestion. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-154](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-154.md) | Reward's effect hinges on its stated contingency | Cameron, Banko and Pierce (2001, [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md)), re-analysing 145 studies with contingencies coded by procedure. On interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermine later free choice when loosely tied to performance (for doing the task, for "doing well") or earned at less than the maximum; they do not when given for surpassing a score, and they enhance it when given for exceeding others. Read through social cognitive and behavioural theory: rewards tied to success carry competence. Proposed: the paper measures no mediator and pools control groups that differ in feedback. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md) | Adaptation needs parts separated by constancies | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md), Chs. 10–16. If all successes must occur at once, trials grow as (1/p)ᴺ; if each is kept once found, roughly as N/p. Keeping one needs no channel from what is still changing to what is already right, so a fully joined system, the Homeostat included, cannot accumulate; constancies cut a system into independent parts. Exact for the type-cases; the fit to brains is qualitative. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-324](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-324.md) v3 | Adaptation needs a second, parameter-changing loop | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md). Necessity is deduced from the trial-and-error rule against a Black Box environment; sufficiency from the theorem that a whole is at equilibrium only where every part is. The Homeostat shows it in a four-unit linear machine. The parameter changes are blind, and the account says nothing about how long the search takes, which is the subject of [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md). | Active |

| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Iterated learners converge to positive linear | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. The bias was taken from earlier studies, not measured on these learners, and stationarity was not established. | [THEORY-688](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-688.md) | Options help only with the right subgoals | Botvinick, Niv and Barto (2009), [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md), read in [NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md). Toy simulations in a rooms domain with pre-trained options. Doorway options sped learning; window options slowed it; with a shortcut opened, primitive-only agents found the shortest path on 75% of runs while doorway-option agents never used it (mean 11.79 against 9.73 steps). It is a result about the model. That people or brains work this way is the separate, proposed account [THEORY-484](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-484.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-895](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-895.md) v2 | Drugs sensitize wanting, not liking | Berridge and Robinson (2016), [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md), read in [NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md) from the PMC author manuscript. | [THEORY-897](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-897.md) v2 | Anxiety alters learning-rate adjustment | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022), [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md), read in full from the NIH author manuscript in [NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md). | [THEORY-934](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-934.md) | Bush–Mosteller drives probability matching | Börgers & Sarin (JET 1997; working paper 1993), [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md), read in full in [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md). | [THEORY-938](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-938.md) | Cross learning converges to pure profiles | Börgers & Sarin (JET 1997; working paper 1993), [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md), read in full from the 1995 working paper in [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md). Two players running Cross's rule with payoffs in (0, 1): expected change equals the discrete replicator step (Proposition 3); the slow-learning limit is the Taylor replicator dynamic at each finite time (Proposition 4); for every step size the process is absorbed in a pure profile with probability one (Proposition 5). The equivalence is pointwise in time, not uniform. | Proposed |

The EEG follow-up re-analyses Experiment 2's participants, so it is no independent replication. The account is behavioural; it does not say people perform Bayesian inference over task-sets, which the authors disclaim, nor that the Chinese-restaurant reuse prior is what people use, which they leave untested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1362](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1362.md) | HGF updates take the same form at every level | Mathys et al. (2014), [LIT-2015](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2015.md), read in [NOTE-1548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1548.md). The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter's update equations for n levels: the same precision-weighted prediction-error form at every level above the first, a value prediction error at level 1 and a volatility prediction error above. Proposed until the updates are re-derived. It says nothing about how close the approximation is to exact inversion, whether the parameters can be recovered, or whether people learn this way. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1363.md) | Shape bias is a learned hyperparameter | Kemp, Perfors & Tenenbaum (2007), [LIT-2017](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2017.md), read in [NOTE-1544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1544.md). Learning a constraint is inference over a hierarchy's higher-level parameters (α, β): low within-category variability of shape is the shape bias. The model reproduces Smith et al.'s first- and second-order generalization qualitatively, with no new experiments, and misses the no-name condition. Computational level; the structure and top prior are given. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1364.md) | Task-set structure shows in prefrontal EEG | Collins, Cavanagh and Frank (2014), [LIT-2007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2007.md), read in [NOTE-1550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1550.md). Proposed: one sample, the participants of Collins and Frank's (2013) Experiment 2 (N = 35; 33 for ERP, 32 for classification), with several uncorrected topographic tests and an early-positivity window chosen from the grand average. The late switch negativity tracked the context dimension but did not predict transfer; the early positivity, absent at group level, and the decoder did (ρ = 0.5, ρ = 0.35), and agreed with each other only marginally. The context dimension is assigned from behavioural switch-costs, so the EEG does not read out the structure independently. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1365.md) | HGF updates take Rescorla–Wagner form | Mathys et al. (2011), [LIT-2016](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2016.md), read in [NOTE-1552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1552.md). A derivation with illustrative simulations: closed-form trial-by-trial updates for a three-level hierarchy of volatility, of Rescorla–Wagner form, with a learning rate that is the agent's posterior variance and grows with its volatility estimate, and with per-agent coupling parameters standing for individual differences. Proposed until the updates are re-derived. It says nothing about how close the approximation is to exact inversion, or about whether people learn this way. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1385.md) | Spaced digital education modestly beats massed | Martinengo, Ng, Ng, Ang, Jabir, Kyaw & Tudor Car (2024), [LIT-2102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2102.md), read in [NOTE-1610](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1610.md): 23 trials, immediate post-intervention outcomes. It does not say that spacing improves retention of skills over months, nor anything about long non-use; and for simulation the abstract and body give different pooled estimates (SMD 1.15 and 1.24). Proposed: one meta-analysis over studies mostly at unclear or high risk of bias. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1404](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1404.md) v3 | Procedural skill decay span is still unknown | Oskar, Prehoda, Sapp, Qi, Botticelli & Palaganas (2026), [LIT-2019](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2019.md), read in [NOTE-1612](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1612.md): a scoping review of 37 studies, with descriptive counts and no quality appraisal. It does not say that emergency procedural skills decay at any particular rate, or that they decay more than other clinicians' skills; it gives no rates at all. Its closing statement of what decay depends on is asserted, not shown. Active as one review's mapping of one specialty's literature; whether another review finds the same gaps is QUESTION-403. | Active |
| [THEORY-1424](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1424.md) v2 | Motor skills decay roughly linearly with disuse | Tatel (2023), [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md), the PhD dissertation behind Tatel & Ackerman (2025), [LIT-2088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2088.md); read in NOTE-1560. A random-effects meta-regression over 457 sources. The slopes are the article abstract's too; the half-loss ranges are the dissertation's (the article gives 6.5, 13 and 11 months). The practice moderator holds for accuracy only, and the author calls the moderators far from definitive. It does not say that decay is linear beyond a year, where data are few, or anything about organizations. Active as a report of one meta-analysis; whether an independent synthesis agrees is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) v4 | Automated subtasks' skills decay unnoticed | Macnamara et al. (2024), [LIT-2224](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2224.md), read in full in [NOTE-1710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1710.md). A theoretical perspective with no data of its own. The decay with disuse, and its being larger for cognitive tasks, are the cited literature's (Arthur et al.; Ackerman and Tatel); the selective loss in pilots is Casner et al. (2014), reported second-hand, without sample or sizes; the concealment is the authors' argument, not a finding. Read as a stand-in for Bainbridge (1983), [LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md), on the skill-decay irony only; the paper does not cite her. It does not give a rate, a recovery time, or any test of its extension to AI assistants. | Active |
| [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) v4 | Train skills before AI, inject AI failures | Ahn (2025), [LIT-2222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2222.md), read in full in [NOTE-1713](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1713.md). The ironies are Ahn's paraphrase of Bainbridge (1983), [LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md), which was not read: he quotes no sentence of hers and gives no page, so this is a THEORY about how she is read, and nothing here is put in her name. The remedies are his proposals for medical curricula, untested. A single-author commentary with no data. | Active |
| [THEORY-1545](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1545.md) | Automated subtask skills decay unnoticed | The thesis the source asserts, split from [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) holds that the authors assert it; whether it is true is this entry's question, under the condition [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1551](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1551.md) | Automation leaves operators the hardest cases | The reading of Bainbridge (1983) that Ahn (2025), [LIT-2222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2222.md), asserts, split from [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) holds that Ahn reads her so; whether she says it turns on her text, which the record holds only as Unavailable ([LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md)), under the condition [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1601](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1601.md) v2 | Planarian memory may survive decapitation | Levin and Shomrat (2013), [LIT-1776](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1776.md), read in [NOTE-1283](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1283.md) (marked Skimmed for its thinness, read in full) in place of Shomrat and Levin 2013 ([LIT-1732](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1732.md)). An automated device trained 12 worms at a time, around the clock, scored by computer, to meet the objections to McConnell's hand-run work. No numbers, methods or controls are given, and the store is said to be unknown. | Active |
| [THEORY-1607](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1607.md) v2 | Synaptic plasticity alone can't explain memory | Blackiston, Shomrat and Levin (2015), [LIT-1707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1707.md), read in [NOTE-1258](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1258.md). A perspective with no new data. It calls the insect mechanism unsolved and the mushroom-body account indirect, and describes the lobe the 2008 moth paper relied on as partly pruned. Its non-synaptic "blueprint" and its bioelectric store are hypotheses; the planarian evidence is the authors' own one-sentence result and a contested 1960s literature. | Active |
| [THEORY-1634](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1634.md) v2 | Caterpillar odour aversion survives metamorphosis | Blackiston, Silva Casey and Weiss (2008), [LIT-1680](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1680.md), read in [NOTE-1249](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1249.md). After fifth-instar odour-shock training, 78% of larvae (N = 41) and 77% of the moths they became (N = 27) avoided ethyl acetate, and 12 of 15 tracked individuals chose alike at both stages. Washing trained pupae or scenting naive ones changed nothing. Third-instar training survived two larval molts (81%, N = 32) and was not expressed by adults (N = 15, a null). The mushroom-body carrier is the authors' hypothesis, not tested. | Active |
| [THEORY-1690](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1690.md) | Tolerance is the hub of problematic porn use | Ince et al. (2024), Problematic pornography use and novel patterns of escalating use, read in [NOTE-1726](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1726.md) (Read). Two cross-sectional online samples of male pornography users (N1 = 1,356 USA; N2 = 944 UK). Measures: the five-item Brief Pornography Screener (BPS) for problematic pornography use (PPU); the PPCS tolerance subscale split into quantitative tolerance (two items, averaged) and qualitative escalation (one item); binge frequency; edging; tab-jumping. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1847](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1847.md) | Automated warfare risks moral deskilling | Vallor (2013), read in full in [NOTE-1926](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1926.md). First-hand stand-in for her 2015 paper ([LIT-2599](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2599.md)) and for the deskilling thesis of The AI Mirror ([LIT-2591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2591.md)). Corroborates [CLAIM-675](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-675.md)'s premise first-hand, which Adewuyi's review ([THEORY-1857](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1857.md)) gave second-hand. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1857](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1857.md) | Algorithmic reliance deskills moral reasoning | Vallor's The AI Mirror as reported in Adewuyi's review (2026), read in [NOTE-1930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1930.md). Mirror; moral deskilling; practical wisdom. It corroborates [CLAIM-675](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-675.md)'s premise, second-hand. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2121.md) | Second-order false belief lags by years | From the reading of [LIT-2895](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2895.md) in [NOTE-2181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2181.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2210](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2210.md) | Withholding avoidance didn't change expectancy | Sridhar, Biagi & Wake (2026), [LIT-3076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3076.md), read in [NOTE-2299](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2299.md). The nearest design [LEAD-047](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-047.md)'s search found to an intervention on what governs action with threat belief measured. Its expectancy null is clean; its avoidance effect is not. Proposed until the avoidance effect is shown confirmatorily. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2211](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2211.md) | Lab motor skills decay faster than real ones | Tatel (2023), [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md), and the coded data posted for Tatel & Ackerman (2025), [LIT-3080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3080.md). For accuracy the decline is 0.16 SD a month on laboratory tasks and about 0.05 on real-world tasks; the dissertation finds "less evidence" that real-world domains differ from one another, and in the posted data medical and dental tasks decline by 0.04 a month while sports and military or transport tasks show no measurable decline over intervals of a year at most. Speed shows the same trend, not significant. Task type is confounded with complexity and with the range of intervals studied. Proposed: one synthesis, by the same author, and the article unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2242](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2242.md) | Safety behaviours didn't hurt spider exposure | Meckes et al. (2025), [LIT-3123](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3123.md), read in [NOTE-2332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2332.md). A randomized test of exposure held fixed with a safety behaviour cut or kept, the design [QUESTION-045](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-045.md) names, with a null on outcome at one month. Proposed until replicated beyond one session and one small sample; it says nothing about cutting a person's own maintaining safety behaviour. | Proposed |
